## Incident Report — NetSupport RAT Infection

**Case:** 2024-11-26 traffic-analysis-exercise
**Evidence:** `2024-11-26-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (26,922 packets, 08:49:38–09:43:58 local/+0400, i.e. 04:49:38–05:43:58 UTC) + Suricata alert export (153 lines)

### Victim host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.11.26.183** |
| MAC address | **d0:57:7b:ce:fc:8b** |
| Windows hostname (NetBIOS) | **DESKTOP-B8TQK49** |
| AD domain | **NEMOTODES.HEALTH** (DC: NEMOTODES-DC.nemotoads.health, 10.11.26.3) |
| Logged-in user | **oboomwald** (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString to 10.11.26.3) |

### Malware family

**NetSupport RAT** — malicious deployment of the legitimate NetSupport Manager remote-access tool, a common payload distributed via fake "cracked software" download sites.

**Attribution: signature-confirmed.** Multiple Suricata rules fired directly on the C2 traffic:
- `ETPRO TROJAN NetSupport RAT CnC Activity` (65 hits)
- `ETPRO TROJAN Malicious NetSupport Rat CnC Checkin` (2 hits)
- `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Checkin` (65 hits) / `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Response` (4 hits)
- `ET POLICY NetSupport GeoLocation Lookup Request`
- `ET POLICY HTTP POST on unusual Port Possibly Hostile` / `ET POLICY HTTP traffic on port 443 (POST)` (HTTP tunneled over TCP/443)

This is corroborated independently by traffic content: every C2 POST carries the literal HTTP User-Agent `NetSupport Manager/1.3`, and the POST bodies use the exact NetSupport client protocol framing `CMD=ENCD\nES=1\nDATA=<encrypted blob>`.

### Indicators of Compromise

**Command-and-control:**
- `194.180.191.64:443` — C2 endpoint. Plaintext HTTP POST (not TLS) to `http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm` disguised on port 443. Beaconing began 2024-11-26 04:50:45 UTC, repeating roughly every 60 seconds, 58 total POSTs through the end of the capture (05:43:29 UTC) — persistent, ongoing C2 session for the full capture duration.

**Malicious/abused domains:**
- `modandcrackedapk.com` → resolved to **193.42.38.139** — flagged by Suricata (`ET CURRENT_EVENTS ZPHP Domain in DNS Lookup` / `...in TLS SNI`); a software-cracking lure site, the likely initial infection vector. All traffic to this domain was TLS-encrypted (TLSv1.2 Client Hellos beginning 04:49:57 UTC), so the dropped payload's filename/hash cannot be recovered from this capture.
- `geo.netsupportsoftware.com` → **104.26.1.231:80**, GET `/location/loca.asp` — NetSupport's own geolocation service, queried by the RAT client immediately before C2 beaconing started (legitimate infrastructure abused by the malware, flagged by Suricata `ET POLICY NetSupport GeoLocation Lookup Request`).

**Malicious URL:**
- `http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm` (C2 checkin endpoint, POST method)

**Transferred files / hashes:**
- No malware executable or installer was observed in cleartext HTTP in this capture — every HTTP object recovered (`connecttest.txt`, `ProcessMAU.txt`, the `fakeurl.htm` C2 exchanges, Microsoft CTL/CryptoAPI downloads) is benign or is the encrypted RAT checkin traffic itself. The actual dropper delivered from `modandcrackedapk.com` traveled inside TLS, so **no file name or SHA256 hash is recoverable from network evidence alone**.

### Supporting/noise alerts (assessed as not part of the compromise)
- SMB/NetBIOS alerts (`EfsRpcOpenFileRaw`, SMBv1 session setup, IPC$ access) between 10.11.26.183 and the domain controller 10.11.26.3 are normal AD/domain-join chatter, not evidence of lateral movement in this capture.
- The Microsoft NCSI, Windows Update, Bing/MSN/Office telemetry, and Adobe update traffic are background OS/application noise, unrelated to the infection.

### Summary
The Windows workstation DESKTOP-B8TQK49 (10.11.26.183, MAC d0:57:7b:ce:fc:8b), logged in as domain user `oboomwald` on NEMOTODES.HEALTH, visited the piracy/cracked-software site `modandcrackedapk.com` (193.42.38.139) around 04:49–04:50 UTC and was infected with **NetSupport RAT**. The malware immediately queried NetSupport's own geolocation service, then established persistent C2 beaconing to **194.180.191.64:443** (HTTP POST to `/fakeurl.htm`, masquerading as TLS on port 443) that continued at ~60-second intervals for the remainder of the capture.
